Be Yourself. Master Your Subject. Think Independently.
Collingham is a small independent GCSE and A Level college in London, built on one idea: students learn best and succeed when they’re known well and trusted to think for themselves.
In practice that means classes of nine or fewer. Two-hour lessons built around discussion, curiosity, and real dialogue between teacher and student. Breadth and depth. Mastery comes from working a subject through for yourself, supported every step by people who know you really well. A community that celebrates and supports students as individuals.
To mark our 50th birthday, we’ve adopted a new symbol: the rhinoceros. In 1515, working only from a sailor’s sketch and a written account, Albrecht Dürer used his own judgement and imagination to draw a rhino, reasoning out its form with real creative flair. His version became the one the world remembered for centuries.
That’s the spirit we’ve carried for fifty years: creativity, careful thinking, and the confidence to trust your own conclusions.
Empowering students to reach their full potential
Our aim is to enable individuals to discover their strengths, set their own goals and develop their full potential and confidence.
At the same time, we are uncompromising in our commitment to academic standards, personal integrity and the development of a sense of responsibility.
Collingham Voices
Alexander
“I joined Collingham from an international school in London because I wanted to do A-Levels and study at a UK university. It’s been a great experience — I completed one of my three A-Levels in Year 12, achieving an A* and am now taking Geography and Politics in Year 13. Collingham is really individual to every student, which has allowed me to continue with all my extracurricular activities alongside my studies.
Nazlican
“One of the things I enjoy most about Collingham is the small class sizes, which allow for individual support from teachers. I also appreciate the cosy atmosphere that makes it easy to settle in. My teachers are passionate about the subjects they teach, and are both attentive and supportive.”
Abella
“I have thoroughly enjoyed my short stay at Collingham; the welcoming and friendly environment, along with the supportive staff and engaging atmosphere, has made it a truly positive and enriching experience.”
Leo
“Collingham for me has been really about the great friends I’ve made along the way. I really like class structure and my tutors have been extraordinarily beneficial.”
Gabriel
“Collingham has been a place where I could really focus, learn, and feel supported. I’m thankful for all of the encouragement along the way.”
Specialist Teachers
Founded in 1975, Collingham is an independent, co-educational school that runs from year 9 through to Sixth Form. Our aim is to enable individuals to discover their strengths, set their own goals and develop their potential and confidence. At the same time, we are uncompromising in our commitment to academic standards, personal integrity and the development of a sense of responsibility. We provide expert tuition, a clear structure of work and a supportive environment.
Leaver Destinations
On average 85% of our students achieved places at their first choice universities. Our students regularly go to the top UK universities, including Oxford, Cambridge, UCL, LSE, Kings College & Durham. We also have several students going to university abroad each year, including the US, Canada & Italy.
Explore University destinations
The City is our Campus
Located in the heart of London’s Royal Borough of Kensington and Chelsea over-looking a beautiful garden square, our school is easily accessible from all parts of London. Our proximity to world-class institutions such as the Victoria & Albert Museum, Imperial College and the Natural History Museum means students have access to unparalleled cultural and academic resources.

Our home for over 50 years and our namesake, 23 Collingham Gardens has been the educational home for the likes of Robert Kennedy, Lord Snowden, Prince Edward, Viscount Linley, and even Christopher Robin Milne, AA Milne’s son and inspiration for the British classic, Winnie the Pooh.
Collingham GCSE
Our GCSE department is housed on Young Street and is steeped in academic pedigree. Previously the residence of William Makepeace Thackeray, where intellectuals such as the Brontë sisters regularly visited for supper.

Famed for its iconic blue whale and dinosaur skeletons, the Natural History Museum is a cornerstone of scientific discovery. With interactive galleries and a rich research legacy, it’s ideal for students intrigued by biology, geology, and environmental science.

Portobello Road Market
Portobello Road Market, established in the 19th century, is renowned as the world’s largest antiques market. It attracts visitors globally, reflecting its vibrant heritage and cultural significance.

A faithful reconstruction of the original Elizabethan playhouse, Shakespeare’s Globe offers powerful open-air performances of the Bard’s works. From its guided tours to educational workshops, it provides an immersive experience of Shakespearean drama just minutes from the City—connecting students directly to literary history.
The National Theatre
Overlooking the Thames, the National Theatre stages bold new plays and timeless classics in striking modernist buildings. Students can experience world-class performances and behind-the-scenes tours, gaining insight into theatre production, design, and dramatic literature—ideal for aspiring creatives, writers, and performers.
Buckingham Palace
The official residence of the monarch, Buckingham Palace is steeped in tradition and pageantry. Its grand façade and ceremonial events offer students a glimpse into constitutional monarchy and British history, making it a landmark of both cultural and educational interest.
Tate Britain
Home to the national collection of British art, Tate Britain spans masterpieces from the 1500s to the present. With regular exhibitions and Turner Prize showcases, it’s a must-visit for students of visual arts, art history, or anyone inspired by British creativity.
The Victoria and Albert Museum
A world leader in art, design, and performance, the V&A showcases everything from Renaissance sculpture to cutting-edge fashion. Its diverse exhibitions and educational resources make it an exceptional learning space for students of history, textiles, art, and architecture.
The Royal Geographical Society
At the heart of exploration and global research, the Royal Geographical Society hosts fascinating exhibitions, lectures, and archives. A hub for students passionate about geography, environmental science, or global affairs, it’s an inspiring destination that bridges academic curiosity with real-world discovery.

Gloucester Road Tube Station
A short walk from both Collingham premises, Gloucester Road Station provides excellent transport links via three Underground lines. Its proximity ensures effortless commuting, while the surrounding area blends residential elegance with convenient shops and cafés—perfect for study breaks or a smooth journey into central London.
South Kensington Tube Station
Just minutes from Collingham’s A-Level and GCSE buildings, South Kensington Station offers swift access across London via the Circle, District, and Piccadilly lines. Ideally placed for daily travel, it also connects students to nearby world-class museums and cultural institutions in the heart of academic Kensington.

Within easy walking distance of Collingham’s GCSE and A-Level centres, High Street Kensington Station connects students to the Circle and District lines. Set amid shops, eateries, and Kensington Gardens, it offers a lively local environment and reliable access to wider London for learning and leisure alike.

Independent Minds Since 1975
Collingham is an independent, co-educational GCSE and Sixth Form college in London, built on one idea: students learn best when they are trusted to think for themselves.
For fifty years, that’s meant classes of nine students or fewer, two-hour lessons built around discussion, and teachers who go by first names, in a place with no uniform to hide behind. Our community consists of around 150 students aged 13 to 19 who join us from a wide range of schools and backgrounds. Some join us for their GCSE years, most arrive at the start of Year 12, and others come to us for a one-year course in Year 14, either to retake a year or to change course, before moving forward with confidence.
How we teach
Be Yourself. Master Your Subject. Think Independently.
Small classes mean every voice gets heard and nowhere to hide. Discussion-based teaching means students test ideas out loud, defend them, and sometimes change their minds. Mastery comes from working a subject through for yourself, supported at every step by staff who know you well and remain uncompromising on academic standards, personal integrity and responsibility.
Where we teach
Our GCSE department, for Years 9 to 11, is based in what was once William Makepeace Thackeray’s house, just off Kensington High Street. He wrote Vanity Fair within these walls, with all three Brontë sisters among his regular guests.
Our Sixth Form sits in Collingham Gardens, a short walk from Gloucester Road and Earls Court, in a historic Arts and Crafts townhouse that has belonged to education for over a century, once home to Gibbs’ Preparatory School. Robert Kennedy, Lord Snowdon, Prince Edward, Viscount Linley and Christopher Robin Milne, the inspiration behind Winnie the Pooh, all passed through these doors before us.
Why the rhino?
To mark our 50th birthday, we adopted a new symbol: a rhinoceros.
In 1515, working only from a sailor’s written account, Albrecht Dürer drew a rhinoceros he had never seen, reasoning out its form through judgement and imagination alone. He got some details wrong, an extra horn, armour-plated skin that isn’t really there, and his version became one of the most reproduced animal images in art history anyway.
That’s the spirit we’ve carried for fifty years: backing your own judgement, thinking a problem through for yourself, and having the confidence to trust your own conclusions, even when they take you somewhere unexpected.
Collingham bridges the best of a small country school with the vibrancy of central London. Come and meet us at an Open Event or book a personal tour, and see what fifty years of independent thinking looks like in practice.

pageCache.pageTitle: A Parent’s Guide to GCSE Courses in London and Kensington - Collingham
pageCache.text:
Choosing GCSE courses is the first major academic decision most students make for themselves. It is also one that parents often find harder to navigate than the students do. The terminology shifts, the options multiply, and the stakes feel high – because they are.
This guide is for parents trying to understand the landscape and help their child choose well.
What GCSE courses are available in London?
The core subjects – English Language, English Literature, Mathematics and the Sciences – are compulsory at most schools and colleges offering GCSE programmes. Beyond those, the range of optional subjects varies considerably between institutions.
Common GCSE options include History, Geography, a modern language (French, Spanish, German, Mandarin), Religious Studies, Art and Design, Drama, Music, Business Studies, Computer Science, Physical Education and Psychology. Some specialist colleges offer additional subjects or alternative qualifications alongside GCSEs.
At Collingham, GCSE students study at the college’s site at 16 Young Street, W8, a short walk from High Street Kensington. The subject range is broad, and the admissions team will discuss availability and suitability with each family before a place is offered.
How many GCSEs should a student take?
Most students take between eight and ten GCSEs. The right number depends on the student. Packing a timetable with ten subjects sounds impressive, but if two or three of those are chosen without much interest or intent, the grades in all of them tend to suffer.
A smaller, more focused set of GCSEs, studied with genuine engagement, will almost always produce better results. The aim is not to accumulate the most subjects but to build the strongest possible foundation for sixth form and beyond.
Core subjects and why they matter
English Language, English Literature and Mathematics are not optional in any meaningful sense. A grade 4 or above in English and Maths is a requirement for progression into most post-16 courses, apprenticeships and employment pathways. Students who do not achieve this in Year 11 will typically need to resit their GCSEs.
The Sciences – Biology, Chemistry and Physics, or Combined Science as a double award – matter particularly for students considering A Level science or medicine. Choosing the right science option at GCSE and studying it properly makes A Level science significantly more manageable.
Choosing optional subjects
The best optional subjects are the ones a student is most likely to engage with seriously over two years. That sounds obvious, but in practice students often choose subjects because friends are taking them, or because a subject sounds interesting without knowing what the coursework and examinations actually involve.
It is worth looking at the full course content, not just the subject title, before deciding. A student who loves reading and discussion may find GCSE History or Religious Studies more rewarding than one who dislikes extended writing but chooses them anyway. A student with a genuine interest in problem-solving may find Computer Science or Further Mathematics more engaging than Business Studies.
At Collingham, subject specialists are available to discuss course content with students and parents before choices are finalised. That conversation often shifts what looks like a clear decision in a different, and better, direction. Book a conversation with the admissions team.
GCSE courses in Kensington
Collingham’s GCSE provision is small by design. Classes are capped at nine students, with an average of five. Teaching is delivered by subject specialists rather than form tutors covering multiple disciplines. The environment is calm and collegiate, without the pressures that come with larger school settings.
Students at Collingham are known by name, by teachers who are genuinely invested in how they are getting on. Pastoral support is built into the programme rather than added on as an afterthought.
The college has been offering GCSE courses in Kensington since 1975. The January 2026 ISI inspection confirmed all standards were met, with inspectors specifically noting the quality of personalised support provided to GCSE students.
What to ask when comparing GCSE providers
How small are the classes? Who does the teaching? Is there flexibility if a student needs to change subjects or adjust their programme? What pastoral support is in place for students who are finding things difficult?
These questions matter as much as the subject list. A GCSE course taken in the right environment, with good teaching and proper support, produces fundamentally different outcomes from the same course taken somewhere larger and less attentive.
Collingham works best for students who need a more personalised approach than a large school can offer – whether that is because they are new to the UK, returning after a gap, managing health or personal circumstances, or simply ready to take their education more seriously in a setting that takes them seriously in return.
If you are looking at GCSE courses in London or Kensington and want to understand whether Collingham is the right fit, the best starting point is a conversation.

Academic Excellence. Individual Focus.
At Collingham Kensington, our A level courses offer a powerful combination of academic rigour, personalised teaching, and a supportive environment that prepares students not only for exam success, but for life at university and beyond.
Whether students join us for a full two-year programme, an intensive one-year course, or to retake selected subjects, our A level provision is flexible, responsive, and tailored to individual goals.

Ancient History
The Subject
This subject provides the student with an insight into the Ancient World, through the study of a variety of sources now available in translation. Not only can one read great historians, such as Herodotus, Thucydides, Livy and Tacitus, but also biographies of Plutarch and the works of Aristotle and Xenophon.
This is a subject which allows students to make up their own minds about past events. Sources have to be evaluated and scrutinised for plausibility and truth. Often one has to come to the uncomfortable conclusion that not everything on a printed page is true! As an A level, it is almost unique in encouraging pupils to question the truth and “spirit” of public pronouncements. There is no better way to understand contemporary politics than to study the uncomfortable world of the ancient Athenian democracy and the Roman Republic and Empire.
No prior knowledge of the ancient world or of classical languages is required to take this course, but students are normally expected to have a good track record in History. Taking Ancient History at A Level makes for an excellent pairing with most subjects, given the breadth of the material studied. In particular, studying the roots of western civilisation and culture will greatly change how you understand later history, literature and politics.
An Ancient History A-level is excellent preparation for a number of degree courses including Law, English, History, Philosophy, and of course, Classics.
Beyond university Classicists have found careers in all walks of life, including banking, teaching, business, journalism and politics. Notable figures who studied classical subjects at university include Charlotte Higgins, Boris Johnson, C. S. Lewis and J. K. Rowling.
The Course
During the course, students explore fifth century Greece and the first dynasty of Roman emperors. We trace the rise and fall of Athens’ empire following the Persians’ unsuccessful invasion of Greece in 480BC, which led towards the great Peloponnesian War between Athens and Sparta in the last three decades of the century. Alongside this period, we will explore the creation of the ‘principate’ in Rome in the wake of the collapse of its Republic, and chart the course of the first dynasty of emperors from the famed Augustus to the despised Nero.
Students then carry on to consider the broader culture and societies of these two ancient civilisations. One module considers the culture and society of classical Athens, including its political structure and festivals. For the Roman half of Year 13, students have the choice of either exploring the collapse of the Republic, or moving on to the politics and exploits of the Flavian dynasty, who came to power in the wake of the civil war following Nero’s assassination.
This qualification is examined by OCR.
Art
Creativity is at the heart of every area of our lives – it is an essential skill that enables us to be effective in all that we do. The Collingham Art Department provides an environment where students can develop and nurture this life affirming skill. Students will learn to develop their own unique approach to the world of the visual arts, refining and improving their ability to experiment with materials and respond to the visual world using the key skills of drawing, painting, printmaking, sculpture and digital media.
The Collingham Art Department is a flourishing centre for the development of the visual arts, enabling students to produce artwork that is both original and technically accomplished. Our staff are committed, inspirational, demanding and fun: given appropriate guidance and sufficient individual attention, all students are capable of producing works of a very high calibre. We achieve a high success rate at both GCSE and A Level and we have a high success rate with entries to foundation and diploma courses at colleges such as Central St. Martins, Chelsea, Camberwell, Wimbledon, Brighton, City and Guilds and the Ruskin School of Art, Oxford.
Feedback from ex-students has time and again showed that, unlike many art departments, our individual and creative approach prepares students to work independently, think for themselves, and develop a mature working method that is invaluable when faced with the demands of Foundation and Degree level Courses.
The purpose-built Art Studio has facilities for drawing, painting, sculpture, printmaking, and various digital media. Research trips are organised to galleries, exhibitions, museums and places of special interest.

Choosing the right GCSE college is one of the most important decisions a family makes. And it is a decision that brochures and websites can only take you so far with. At some point, you need to sit down with someone who actually knows the college, ask the questions that are genuinely on your mind, and get straight answers.
That is what the Head’s Coffee is for.
What is the Head’s Coffee?
The Head’s Coffee is a small, informal morning session hosted by Paul, Head of GCSE at Collingham. It takes place at the GCSE building at 16 Young Street, W8 – a short walk from High Street Kensington – and runs from 9.30am to 10.30am.
Sessions run across the academic year and are kept deliberately small – around 15 people, which typically means three or four families. That is the point. It is not a presentation to a room full of strangers. It is a conversation.
Current parents and students are present, which means you get to hear directly from families who have already been through the process, and from students who are in the middle of it. The questions they answer are the ones that actually matter: what is it really like? What was the transition like? Would they do it again?
Who is Paul?
Paul is Head of GCSE at Collingham and knows every GCSE student by name. The pastoral structure of the GCSE programme runs through him. He is the person who would be most involved in your child’s journey at Collingham, and the Head’s Coffee is your chance to meet him properly before making any decisions.
He will talk through how the GCSE programme works, what Collingham expects of its students, and what students and families can expect from the college in return. There is no script. If a question occurs to you, ask it.
What makes the Collingham GCSE different
The GCSE community at Collingham is a tight group based at 16 Young Street, W8 – a building with its own distinct identity. The site was once the home of William Makepeace Thackeray, who wrote Vanity Fair within these walls, with all three Bronte sisters among his regular guests. It is a calm, collegiate environment that does not feel like a school in the conventional sense.
Classes are capped at nine students, with an average of five. Teaching is delivered by subject specialists. There are no large year groups, no corridors full of noise, no uniform. Students are expected to take responsibility for their own learning from the start, with guidance and pastoral support built in at every step.
The January 2026 ISI inspection confirmed all standards were met, with inspectors specifically noting the strength of the college’s personalised support for GCSE students.
Is this the right fit for your child?
Collingham’s GCSE programme works best for students who need something different from what a large secondary school offers – whether that is because of how they learn, how they are taught, or the environment they need to thrive in. Some students join in Year 9, some in Year 10, and some come specifically to resit one or more GCSE subjects.
Whatever the reason, the Head’s Coffee is the best way to find out whether Collingham is right for your family. Not a prospectus. A proper conversation, over coffee, with the person who leads the programme.

The Head’s Coffee takes place at our GCSE building at 16 Young Street, London W8 5EL. The nearest station is High Street Kensington (Circle and District lines), a short walk away. Street parking is available nearby.

pageCache.pageTitle: Your Options for A Level Courses in London and Kensington - Collingham
pageCache.text:
Choosing A Level courses is one of the most consequential decisions a student will make. Get it right and the next two years build genuine momentum. Get it wrong and the subjects feel like a grind, the grades suffer, and the university application is weaker for it.
In London, students have more options than almost anywhere else in the country. More colleges, more subjects, more combinations. That breadth is valuable, but it also makes the decision harder. This is a practical guide to understanding your options.
What A Level courses are available in London?
Most sixth forms and independent colleges in London offer the core A Level subjects: Mathematics, Further Mathematics, Biology, Chemistry, Physics, English Literature, History, Geography, Economics, Business Studies, Psychology and the main modern languages. Beyond those, provision varies considerably.
Specialist and independent colleges tend to offer a wider range, including subjects like Politics, Philosophy, Sociology, Law, Art and Design, Photography, Media Studies, Drama and Music. At Collingham, the full range of A Level subjects is broad, and the admissions team will always have a direct conversation about whether a particular combination works for a student’s goals.
How many A Levels should a student take?
The standard is three A Levels, and for most university applications three strong grades are worth far more than four average ones. Some students take four, particularly those applying to highly competitive courses or institutions that specify a fourth subject. A very small number take two, usually in specific circumstances where a different programme structure makes more sense.
The quality of teaching and the student’s engagement with the subjects matter far more than the number of subjects chosen. Three A Levels, taught well, in subjects a student genuinely cares about, will almost always produce better outcomes than a broader programme that spreads effort too thin.
Choosing the right subjects
The most important question is not which subjects look best on a UCAS application but which subjects will this student work hardest in. University admissions tutors are experienced at reading personal statements and predicted grades. A student who has chosen subjects they find genuinely interesting is almost always more compelling than one who has picked strategically but without conviction.
That said, some courses and careers do require specific A Levels, and it is worth checking entry requirements early. Medicine and Dentistry typically require Chemistry and Biology. Engineering programmes often require Mathematics and Physics. Law, Politics and similar humanities courses tend to be more flexible.
If there is any ambiguity, speak to the college’s admissions team before finalising subject choices. At Collingham, that conversation happens at the start of the process, not as an afterthought. Get in touch to arrange a conversation.
What a difference the right environment makes
It is easy to focus on subject choices and miss the thing that matters most: where a student learns, and how well they are known there.
Maddie came to Collingham after receiving grades that disappointed her. Her school encouraged her to accept Clearing and settle for less. She did not.
“I knew those grades did not reflect my ability or my potential, and I wasn’t ready to give up on achieving what I knew I was capable of.”
She retook Biology and Maths, added English Literature in a single year, and left with A*A*A. Some of the first people she told about her Oxford offer were the staff at Collingham.
“Collingham gave me the confidence to aim high and the independence to find the systems and approaches that worked best for me. Those are lessons I still carry with me today.”
Maddie is now reading Law at the University of Oxford.
Her story is not unusual at Collingham. What is consistent is the pattern: a student who needed a different environment, found one, and discovered what they were actually capable of. The subject choices mattered. The teaching mattered. But the thing that changed everything was being somewhere small enough for someone to notice. If you are considering an A Level retake, it is worth understanding what that environment can do.
A Level courses in Kensington
Collingham has been offering A Level courses from its Kensington base since 1975. The college operates across two townhouses in the Royal Borough of Kensington and Chelsea, a short walk from High Street Kensington. Classes are capped at nine students, with an average of five, and teaching is delivered by subject specialists rather than generalists.
The timetable is built around the student, not the other way around. Students can combine subjects across different year groups, adjust their programme if circumstances change, and access individual support from their personal tutor throughout the year.
For students who need to retake one or more A Levels alongside new subjects, or who are starting an A Level course after a different educational pathway, Collingham’s flexible structure makes that straightforward.
What to look for when comparing A Level colleges
Beyond subject range, the questions worth asking are: how small are the classes? Who does the teaching? What happens if a student is struggling and needs additional support? What is the college’s track record with university applications?
A large sixth form with a broad subject offer is not automatically better than a smaller college with fewer subjects but far more personalised provision. The right environment for one student may be entirely wrong for another, and the best colleges are honest about that rather than trying to be everything to everyone.
Collingham’s ISI inspection in January 2026 confirmed all standards were met, with inspectors noting the strength of personalised support and the quality of teaching across subjects.
If you are exploring A Level courses in London or Kensington and want to understand whether Collingham is the right fit, start with a conversation.

Kensington is not short of options when it comes to A Level education. There are sixth forms attached to large secondary schools, independent colleges, private tutoring centres and everything in between. So what actually separates a great A Level college from one that is simply convenient?
This is a question worth taking seriously, because the answer matters more than most families realise when they first start looking.
Size
The single biggest difference between a great A Level college and an average one is often the simplest: how many students are in the room. In a class of twenty-five, it is possible to go an entire lesson without being challenged, without asking a question, without anyone noticing whether you have understood something or not. In a class of eight, that is not possible.
Small classes are not just a comfort feature. They change the quality of learning fundamentally. They create the conditions for real dialogue between student and teacher, for questions to be asked and properly answered, for gaps in understanding to be caught early rather than discovered in an exam hall.
At Collingham, A Level classes are capped at eight students, with an average of five. That is not a marketing figure. It is a structural commitment to the kind of teaching that actually works.
Teaching quality
Class size only matters if the teaching inside it is good. The best A Level colleges in Kensington employ subject specialists, not generalists covering multiple disciplines. There is a difference between a teacher who knows their subject well enough to deliver a syllabus and one who is genuinely expert, genuinely curious, and genuinely invested in each student’s progress.
At Collingham, tutors are subject specialists, many of them active practitioners in their fields. They bring depth and enthusiasm to what they teach, and students notice the difference.
Flexibility
Not every A Level student fits neatly into a standard timetable. Some are managing health conditions or personal circumstances. Some are elite athletes or performers balancing training commitments with study. Some simply learn better at certain times of day, or need a programme that combines subjects across different levels.
A great A Level college builds its timetable around its students rather than expecting students to fit around it. At Collingham, flexible timetabling is not an exception for unusual cases – it is standard practice, available to everyone from the start.
Environment
Where a student learns matters. Collingham operates from two Kensington townhouses – calm, spacious, adult environments that feel collegiate rather than institutional. There are no corridors full of younger pupils, no bells, no uniform. Students are treated as young adults from day one, which tends to bring out the best in them.
The college sits in the Royal Borough of Kensington and Chelsea, a short walk from High Street Kensington. For families based in West London, it is genuinely local. For those coming from further afield, it is easy to reach.
Pastoral support
Academic results matter. But the environment that produces them matters too. The best A Level colleges know their students as individuals, not as names on a register. They have systems in place to notice when something is wrong, to respond quickly, and to support students through the pressures that inevitably come with A Level study.
Collingham’s ISI inspection in January 2026 confirmed all standards were met, with inspectors specifically noting the quality of personalised support. Every student at Collingham has a personal tutor and access to dedicated pastoral care throughout the year.
Outcomes
Ultimately, a great A Level college produces great results. Not by drilling students through past papers, but by building genuine understanding, independent thinking and the confidence to perform under pressure. Collingham students progress to universities across the UK and internationally, including Russell Group institutions, art colleges, conservatoires and competitive professional programmes.
If you are weighing up A Level options in Kensington and want to understand whether Collingham is the right fit, the best place to start is a conversation.
What makes Collingham different
Fifty years in Kensington. Classes capped at eight. Subject specialists who know their students by name. A timetable that fits the student, not the other way around. Independent thinking encouraged from day one.
That is not a list of features. It is a philosophy – one that has been in place since 1975 and has not changed because it works.

Ancient History
The Subject
This subject provides the student with an insight into the Ancient World, through the study of a variety of sources now available in translation. Not only can one read great historians, such as Herodotus, Thucydides, Livy and Tacitus, but also biographies of Plutarch and the works of Aristotle and Xenophon.
This is a subject which allows students to make up their own minds about past events. Sources have to be evaluated and scrutinised for plausibility and truth. Often one has to come to the uncomfortable conclusion that not everything on a printed page is true! As an A level, it is almost unique in encouraging pupils to question the truth and “spirit” of public pronouncements. There is no better way to understand contemporary politics than to study the uncomfortable world of the ancient Athenian democracy and the Roman Republic and Empire.
No prior knowledge of the ancient world or of classical languages is required to take this course, but students are normally expected to have a good track record in History. Taking Ancient History at A Level makes for an excellent pairing with most subjects, given the breadth of the material studied. In particular, studying the roots of western civilisation and culture will greatly change how you understand later history, literature and politics.
An Ancient History A-level is excellent preparation for a number of degree courses including Law, English, History, Philosophy, and of course, Classics.
Beyond university Classicists have found careers in all walks of life, including banking, teaching, business, journalism and politics. Notable figures who studied classical subjects at university include Charlotte Higgins, Boris Johnson, C. S. Lewis and J. K. Rowling.
The Course
During the course, students explore fifth century Greece and the first dynasty of Roman emperors. We trace the rise and fall of Athens’ empire following the Persians’ unsuccessful invasion of Greece in 480BC, which led towards the great Peloponnesian War between Athens and Sparta in the last three decades of the century. Alongside this period, we will explore the creation of the ‘principate’ in Rome in the wake of the collapse of its Republic, and chart the course of the first dynasty of emperors from the famed Augustus to the despised Nero.
Students then carry on to consider the broader culture and societies of these two ancient civilisations. One module considers the culture and society of classical Athens, including its political structure and festivals. For the Roman half of Year 13, students have the choice of either exploring the collapse of the Republic, or moving on to the politics and exploits of the Flavian dynasty, who came to power in the wake of the civil war following Nero’s assassination.
This qualification is examined by OCR.
Art
Creativity is at the heart of every area of our lives – it is an essential skill that enables us to be effective in all that we do. The Collingham Art Department provides an environment where students can develop and nurture this life affirming skill. Students will learn to develop their own unique approach to the world of the visual arts, refining and improving their ability to experiment with materials and respond to the visual world using the key skills of drawing, painting, printmaking, sculpture and digital media.
The Collingham Art Department is a flourishing centre for the development of the visual arts, enabling students to produce artwork that is both original and technically accomplished. Our staff are committed, inspirational, demanding and fun: given appropriate guidance and sufficient individual attention, all students are capable of producing works of a very high calibre. We achieve a high success rate at both GCSE and A Level and we have a high success rate with entries to foundation and diploma courses at colleges such as Central St. Martins, Chelsea, Camberwell, Wimbledon, Brighton, City and Guilds and the Ruskin School of Art, Oxford.
Feedback from ex-students has time and again showed that, unlike many art departments, our individual and creative approach prepares students to work independently, think for themselves, and develop a mature working method that is invaluable when faced with the demands of Foundation and Degree level Courses.
The purpose-built Art Studio has facilities for drawing, painting, sculpture, printmaking, and various digital media. Research trips are organised to galleries, exhibitions, museums and places of special interest.

The Subject
Chemistry at Collingham is a rewarding academic experience, developing both theoretical understanding and practical experimental skills in a successful, vibrant department.
Why study Chemistry?
Chemistry is the study of matter. It looks at the structures of molecules that comprise all matter, and the fundamental principles which define the appearance, behaviour and changes that molecules undergo. Molecules may be large or small, simple or complex, short-lived or inert, life-saving or fatal…. Some are even beautiful. As the Royal Society of Chemistry asserts, “Chemistry is everything”, from the microscopic world of atoms and molecules to the macroscopic world of stars and galaxies.
Chemistry is pivotal to Science. It links with Physics to understand the fundamental chemical and physical processes in our universe and with Biological Sciences to understand the processes of life itself. The study of Chemistry can lead to a wide range of careers, from Medicine and Pharmaceuticals to the manufacturing industries, to the protection and destruction of our environment and even to the Arts, for instance art restoration or science fiction and crime novels. Chemistry also gives access to Engineering, Forensic Science, Agricultural Studies, Accountancy and even Journalism.

The students’ practical competency will be reported by Edexcel on Paper 4.
Chemistry provides students with a range of skills, at the centre of which is the logical and critical analysis of any problem. Learning and problem-solving take place within a stimulating academic environment. The course makes available to the student the factual knowledge required for the subject and discusses its underlying principles and theories in a form which always encourages the students to think for themselves.
All lessons are carefully planned and delivered in a format that is the one most appropriate for meeting the scientific needs of the particular group and its individual members. Laboratory work is judiciously chosen to extend the students’ understanding of theory as well as developing their practical skills; this is in conjunction with the minimum of twelve of the sixteen core practicals specified by Edexcel. A Second Chance to Succeed
At Collingham College, in Kensington London, we believe that one set of exam results should never define a student’s future. Our A Level Retake courses are designed to help students significantly improve their grades, rebuild confidence, and secure entry to their chosen university or course.
We offer flexible, supportive, and high-impact teaching that focuses on progress, performance, and personal growth. Whether a student needs to retake one subject or several, our team will design a tailored programme to meet their specific needs.
Tangible Results
In 2025, students on our A Level retake programme improved by an average of 1.24 grades per subject, with 88% improving their result and more than one in three achieving a two-grade improvement.
Why Retake A Levels at Collingham College?
Students are supported by dedicated tutors and a personal tutor who oversees both academic progress and wellbeing.
Expert teaching from experienced subject specialists

A Level Resit FAQs
Can I resit just one A level?
Yes. Whether you need to retake one subject or several, we’ll design a tailored programme around your specific needs rather than putting everyone through the same course.
What is Year 14?
Year 14 is Collingham’s dedicated year for students re-sitting A levels or taking a new A level in one year, rather than two. Most schools finish at Year 13, so students who need extra time or a fresh attempt are often left with nowhere proper to go. Year 14 is built for exactly that: focused teaching, a class of students in the same position, and tutors who know how to get a full course covered well in twelve months.
Do I have to resit the whole A level, or just the parts I did badly on?
The whole A level. Under the current linear system you sit all the exam papers again, in one sitting, in May or June. The one exception is non-exam assessment (coursework), which can sometimes be carried forward. Your subject teacher will tell you what applies to you.
How long does an A level retake take?
It depends on what you need. Options include a full one-year course, a short intensive course (for example, starting in January or just the Spring Term), or additional tuition alongside a gap year and work experience. We’ll work out which shape suits you.
When can I start an A level resit at Collingham?
We accept applications on a rolling basis. Most students start in September, but short courses can begin in January or straight after mock results, and many students join us just after their August results come out.
Will resitting affect my university application?
No. Admissions tutors see resit grades every year. What they’re looking for is the final grade on your UCAS form, and evidence that you’ve worked hard to get there. A retake year, done properly, often produces a stronger personal statement, not a weaker one.
Can I combine a retake with a new A level subject?
Yes, this is common. Some students use their retake year to add a subject that strengthens a particular university course, while resitting the grade that’s holding them back.
What subjects can I resit at A level?
Retake options cover a wide range of subjects, including Mathematics and Further Mathematics, Biology, Chemistry, Physics, English Literature, History, Politics, Geography, Economics, Business Studies, Psychology, Sociology, French, Spanish, Latin, Art, Photography and Media Studies. See our full subject list and exam boards for details.
What size are the classes?
Small enough to matter. Group sizes average five students, with a maximum of nine, and individual tuition is available where it’s the better fit.
How many hours of tuition will I get?
Year 14 students get 7 hours of teaching per subject each week (8 for Chemistry, 4 for one-to-one). You’ll have regular Personal Tutor meetings arranged as needed, and independent study should add roughly the same number of hours again per subject.
On the two-year A level programme, Year 12 students get 5 hours per subject (3 if 1-to-1), two 2-hour supervised study periods, one hour of Selfhood (PSHE) and 1 to 2 hours of Friday afternoon activities. Year 13 students get 6 hours per subject (4 if 1-to-1).
What exam boards do you use?
Generally we’ll keep you on the exam board you originally studied, and our tutors can teach all the major boards. Occasionally it’s better to switch, and we’ll say so if that’s the case. Talk to us and we’ll give you honest advice based on your specific subjects.
Do you offer A level retakes as a private candidate?
We allow private external candidates to sit exams with us, but only if they’ve had some tuition from us first. This usually means a minimum of twenty hours, though it can vary by candidate and subject. Get in touch and we’ll talk through what would apply to you.
What happens on results day if I need to resit?
Come and see us. We’ll go through your options there and then, calmly, and help you decide whether a re-sit, a different subject combination, or a different path altogether is the right next step. You don’t need to have an answer on the day itself.
Why choose a sixth form college over resitting at my old school?
Most schools stop at Year 13. Collingham offers a focused Year 14 built specifically for students who want to re-sit or take an A level in one year. You’ll be alongside others in the same position, taught by tutors who know how to cover a course properly in twelve months, not stretch it thin.
I narrowly missed my grade. Should I ask for a review of marking instead of resitting?
It’s worth doing both in parallel rather than choosing one. A review can take weeks with no guarantee of a changed grade. Enrolling for a re-sit at the same time means you’re not losing preparation time while you wait. Talk to us and we’ll help you weigh up whether a review is worth pursuing for your specific paper.
Do I get support with reapplying to university?
Yes. Retake students get structured UCAS guidance, including personal statement writing and improvement, university reapplication advice, Oxbridge and competitive course strategy, and preparation for entrance exams and admissions conversations.
How can you help me with UCAS if you don't know me yet?
By the time you need a reference and predicted grades, you won’t be a stranger to us. Your teachers will have marked your work, sat with you in class, and watched how you handle the material for months. What’s different in a Year 14 reference is that we can speak honestly about what happened the first time and what’s changed, which often makes for a more convincing UCAS application, not a weaker one.
Do you have success stories from students who've taken resits?
Yes, plenty. Success looks different for every student. For some it’s Oxford or Cambridge. For others it’s art college, a degree apprenticeship, or something else entirely. One graduate went on to work on rollercoaster design at Alton Towers. You’re an individual with your own backstory and your own goals. We want to help you get there.
What grades do I need to enrol?
There’s no blanket grade requirement. Some subjects have a recommended GCSE starting point (Maths and Economics generally need a good GCSE in Maths; humanities generally need a good GCSE in English), but we look at individual circumstances rather than applying these as strict cut-offs. Every student starts with an academic consultation where we build a personalised re-take plan and advise honestly on whether the course is the right fit.
What if I'm not currently at school or college, for example after a gap year?
That’s not a problem. We take students straight from school, students returning after time away, and students who’ve been studying independently. Get in touch and we’ll talk through where you are and what a Year 14 place would involve for you.
Is there an age limit to join Collingham?
Yes. Collingham is licensed to accept students up to the age of 19, so you can’t be over 20 when you join us.
How much does an A level retake cost?
See our fees page for current course fees.
I already have access arrangements. Will these carry over?
Access arrangements have to be reassessed at each new centre, based on evidence of how you normally work, so they don’t automatically transfer. Bring us whatever evidence and reports you already have as early as possible and we’ll get the process started well before exam entry deadlines.
How do I apply?
Contact the Admissions Team and arrange a consultation and meeting with our Principal, James Allder, or other senior members of the team. International applicants can join by video call. Call 020 7244 7414 or complete our enquiry form below.
